Imagine two colleagues who both keep a clear record of what they agreed with a client. That can reflect experience, a requirement of their jobs or a shared preference for structure. The behaviour is insufficient to assign either type.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: reading the same request for a quote

In a fictional procurement review, two colleagues receive the same form, figures and deadline. It is unclear whether three fields include tax, freight and the warranty start date. Both can ask for clarification, and neither can change the terms or send a final quote without approval.

One concern is what the difference would mean for the client and the staff relying on the figures. Another is whether the same definitions and comparison rules can be applied to each proposed entry. Both colleagues can consider both questions.

body: **Framework sources.** The [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts) explains the four preferences. The Foundation’s [type dynamics explanation](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) explains how they interact, and its [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/) lists the positions and tertiary alternatives.
**Function notation.** This article uses Fe–Si–Ne–Ti for ESFJ and Si–Te–Fi–Ne for ISTJ. The Foundation also lists Ni for ESFJ’s tertiary Intuition and Fe for ISTJ’s tertiary Feeling.

**Fictional examples.** The procurement form, quote, shorter deadline and request for trade pricing are invented. They illustrate how people might weigh a decision and provide no evidence about anyone’s type.

**Scope.** Preference descriptions cannot rank ability, screen applicants or predict relationships. FermatMind uses its own questionnaire and scoring, described in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

comparison.summary:
ESFJ and ISTJ share Sensing (S) and Judging (J). They differ on Extraversion and Introversion (E/I) and on Thinking and Feeling (T/F). Both profiles emphasise concrete information and experience, and both favour structure in the outside world. Those preferences alone cannot establish reliability or skill.

- **E/I.** ESFJ’s E describes attention and energy directed outward. ISTJ’s I describes attention and energy directed inward. Either person can talk through a problem or take time to reflect.
- **T/F.** ESFJ’s F emphasises values and effects on people. ISTJ’s T emphasises logical consistency and criteria that can be applied across cases. Either person can weigh both considerations.

Under the convention used here, ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. ESFJ leads with extraverted Feeling (Fe) and uses introverted Sensing (Si) as auxiliary. ISTJ leads with Si and uses extraverted Thinking (Te) as auxiliary. Both stacks show Ne in different positions under this tertiary convention.

When reviewing the same quote, either type could ask how a client will use it or check where each figure came from. The order may reflect the person’s role, authority or deadline. It cannot establish a type.

compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
Within each fictional situation, both colleagues have the same information, authority and deadline. Each row illustrates one preference or a shared aspect of the task. Either colleague can use the approach in either column.

| Shared situation | ESFJ: possible emphasis | ISTJ: possible emphasis | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both review the same mismatch in quote definitions | Weigh how each available definition would affect the people using the quote | Weigh whether the same definitions would give a consistent basis for comparison | T/F: effects on people or consistently applied criteria |
| Both receive the same clarification from the client | Think through what it means by discussing it with a colleague | Think through what it means by reflecting privately | E/I: outward engagement or inward reflection |
| The same deadline moves forward by ten days | Weigh how each feasible schedule would affect staff and the people awaiting delivery | Apply the same agreed capacity and commitments criteria to each feasible schedule | T/F: effects on people or consistency across options |
| A regular client requests the same exception | Consider what approving or declining it would mean for the people involved | Consider whether either decision follows criteria that could be applied to comparable cases | T/F: effects on people or consistent criteria |
| Both investigate the same discrepancy | Check what the records and delivery dates confirm | Check what the same records and delivery dates confirm | Shared S: attention to concrete facts |
| The same document is ready for review | Agree on a final version, sign-off and a time to send it | Agree on the same final version, sign-off and time to send it | Shared J: both can prefer an explicit arrangement |

Someone trained to reconcile quotes may check every source before discussing terms. A person assigned to contact the client may call first. Role and experience can explain both, and no row can establish a type.
compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Imagine two colleagues who both keep a clear record of what they agreed with a client. That can reflect experience, a requirement of their jobs or a shared preference for structure. The behaviour is insufficient to assign either type.

The shared S and J concern different parts of the work. Sensing can show up in the importance given to confirmed details, such as a shipment date or a line from a previous quote. Judging can show up in a preference for confirming the plan and documenting who owns the next step.

E/I concerns where attention goes while working on a problem. T/F concerns the reasons someone uses to make a decision. A person can reflect privately and give weight to a customer’s circumstances, or talk an idea through and apply the same criteria across suppliers.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: reading the same request for a quote

In a fictional procurement review, two colleagues receive the same form, figures and deadline. It is unclear whether three fields include tax, freight and the warranty start date. Both can ask for clarification, and neither can change the terms or send a final quote without approval.

One concern is what the difference would mean for the client and the staff relying on the figures. Another is whether the same definitions and comparison rules can be applied to each proposed entry. Both colleagues can consider both questions.

A form may be easy to read and still contain figures that cannot be compared. A traceable figure can also be misunderstood if its definition is missing. These are gaps to check regardless of who prepared the form.

The same person could ask the client a question or trace a figure first. Either task can be useful. The reason to choose it may come from the ambiguity in the form or from the role, without telling you what the person would prefer in another setting.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: why shared Si sits in different positions

Both types have J, which points to an outward-facing judging function. For ESFJ, F identifies it as Fe, and E puts it in the dominant position. For ISTJ, T identifies it as Te, and I puts it in the auxiliary position. That leaves inward-facing Si dominant for ISTJ and auxiliary for ESFJ.

Under the notation used here, Ne is tertiary for ESFJ and inferior for ISTJ. ESFJ’s inferior judging function is Ti, and ISTJ’s tertiary judging function is Fi. Sharing the letter S or the Si function does not mean two people will select the same evidence or reach the same decision.

The Foundation lists Intuition (Ne or Ni) as ESFJ’s tertiary function and Feeling (Fe or Fi) as ISTJ’s. Under this article’s convention the two stacks share Si and Ne. The overlap would change with different tertiary orientations.

The positions describe the theory. They do not predict who communicates more effectively or who will produce a better quote. See the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj) for the four preferences in each type.
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
The following fictional examples illustrate how people might weigh the same decision. Real quotes, discounts and delivery commitments depend on the agreement and on who can approve them.

When sharing the work, decide who checks the figures, who confirms definitions and who sends the approved version. Assign those responsibilities by access and experience.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: two ways to submit the same quote

In a fictional procurement review, a client points out that three suppliers have used different definitions. Both colleagues see the same quote, template and deadline. Neither can publish unapproved figures.

If the client agrees that a partial submission would help, one option is to send only confirmed and approved figures in its format, label the unresolved fields and set a time to follow up. Another is to agree on the definitions before sending a complete quote. Either person can propose either option.

Consider both what the client can use now and how the final figures will be checked. A partial quote can be useful if its limits are clear. Waiting can avoid comparing figures with different meanings, but it may leave the client without the information they need for a meeting.

Record which definitions are agreed, which figures were cleared for release and who will resolve each question. This tests the quality of the handover. It cannot identify someone as ESFJ or ISTJ.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: a relative asks about trade pricing

In a fictional supply business, a relative who runs a small grocery shop asks about trade pricing and an invoice. Two colleagues have the same information and the same authority to refer the request for review. Neither can approve a discount.

One concern is how granting or refusing an exception would affect the relative, other customers and colleagues. Another is how the same criteria would apply to comparable requests. Either employee can consider both before explaining what is possible.

Either person can decline a request they cannot approve and, where appropriate, explain the usual route for checking eligibility. The way they phrase that answer does not reveal how much they care.

The two colleagues could reach the same decision for different reasons, or include both reasons. The example shows what each consideration would add, without assigning that consideration to a type.

compare_blocks.body:
A person can care how a decision affects a client and still want the same criteria applied across cases. An ISTJ’s Thinking preference does not describe their warmth, and an ESFJ’s Feeling preference does not say whether they will make an exception.

Both people can hold to a definition or refer a special case for approval. Knowing who has authority and what the rules allow matters more than inferring a preference from the outcome.

A careful table may reflect training, a template or the demands of an audit. It does not establish a preference.

Calling first or checking records first can depend on what information is missing, how much time remains and who is responsible for the reply. Either type can do both.

faq_blocks.answer:

faq_blocks.answer:
Yes. The work depends on checking figures, clarifying definitions and communicating decisions. Assign it according to access, authority and skill.

faq_blocks.answer:

If a partial submission is appropriate, send only verified figures cleared for release. Mark the missing fields and explain when you expect to complete them. This can work for either type.

faq_blocks.answer:
They differ on E/I and T/F. Compare how the instruments ask about those preferences and whether you had similar situations in mind when you answered.

If the instrument explains its scores and cutoffs, use its guidance to interpret the result. The labels alone cannot tell you how close either score was to a threshold. Keep the distinction between what a role required and what you would choose in similar circumstances.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Imagine two colleagues who both keep a clear record of what they agreed with a client. That can reflect experience, a requirement of their jobs or a shared preference for structure. The behaviour is insufficient to assign either type.

The shared S and J concern different parts of the work. Sensing can show up in the importance given to confirmed details, such as a shipment date or a line from a previous quote. Judging can show up in a preference for confirming the plan and documenting who owns the next step.

E/I concerns where attention goes while working on a problem. T/F concerns the reasons someone uses to make a decision. A person can reflect privately and give weight to a customer’s circumstances, or talk an idea through and apply the same criteria across suppliers.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: reading the same request for a quote

In a fictional procurement review, two colleagues receive the same form, figures and deadline. It is unclear whether three fields include tax, freight and the warranty start date. Both can ask for clarification, and neither can change the terms or send a final quote without approval.

One concern is what the difference would mean for the client and the staff relying on the figures. Another is whether the same definitions and comparison rules can be applied to each proposed entry. Both colleagues can consider both questions.

A form may be easy to read and still contain figures that cannot be compared. A traceable figure can also be misunderstood if its definition is missing. These are gaps to check regardless of who prepared the form.

The same person could ask the client a question or trace a figure first. Either task can be useful. The reason to choose it may come from the ambiguity in the form or from the role, without telling you what the person would prefer in another setting.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: why shared Si sits in different positions

Both types have J, which points to an outward-facing judging function. For ESFJ, F identifies it as Fe, and E puts it in the dominant position. For ISTJ, T identifies it as Te, and I puts it in the auxiliary position. That leaves inward-facing Si dominant for ISTJ and auxiliary for ESFJ.

Under the notation used here, Ne is tertiary for ESFJ and inferior for ISTJ. ESFJ’s inferior judging function is Ti, and ISTJ’s tertiary judging function is Fi. Sharing the letter S or the Si function does not mean two people will select the same evidence or reach the same decision.

The Foundation lists Intuition (Ne or Ni) as ESFJ’s tertiary function and Feeling (Fe or Fi) as ISTJ’s. Under this article’s convention the two stacks share Si and Ne. The overlap would change with different tertiary orientations.

The positions describe the theory. They do not predict who communicates more effectively or who will produce a better quote. See the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj) for the four preferences in each type.

sections.body_md:
Within each fictional situation, both colleagues have the same information, authority and deadline. Each row illustrates one preference or a shared aspect of the task. Either colleague can use the approach in either column.

| Shared situation | ESFJ: possible emphasis | ISTJ: possible emphasis | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both review the same mismatch in quote definitions | Weigh how each available definition would affect the people using the quote | Weigh whether the same definitions would give a consistent basis for comparison | T/F: effects on people or consistently applied criteria |
| Both receive the same clarification from the client | Think through what it means by discussing it with a colleague | Think through what it means by reflecting privately | E/I: outward engagement or inward reflection |
| The same deadline moves forward by ten days | Weigh how each feasible schedule would affect staff and the people awaiting delivery | Apply the same agreed capacity and commitments criteria to each feasible schedule | T/F: effects on people or consistency across options |
| A regular client requests the same exception | Consider what approving or declining it would mean for the people involved | Consider whether either decision follows criteria that could be applied to comparable cases | T/F: effects on people or consistent criteria |
| Both investigate the same discrepancy | Check what the records and delivery dates confirm | Check what the same records and delivery dates confirm | Shared S: attention to concrete facts |
| The same document is ready for review | Agree on a final version, sign-off and a time to send it | Agree on the same final version, sign-off and time to send it | Shared J: both can prefer an explicit arrangement |

Someone trained to reconcile quotes may check every source before discussing terms. A person assigned to contact the client may call first. Role and experience can explain both, and no row can establish a type.
sections.title: ESFJ and ISTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
The following fictional examples illustrate how people might weigh the same decision. Real quotes, discounts and delivery commitments depend on the agreement and on who can approve them.

When sharing the work, decide who checks the figures, who confirms definitions and who sends the approved version. Assign those responsibilities by access and experience.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: two ways to submit the same quote

In a fictional procurement review, a client points out that three suppliers have used different definitions. Both colleagues see the same quote, template and deadline. Neither can publish unapproved figures.

If the client agrees that a partial submission would help, one option is to send only confirmed and approved figures in its format, label the unresolved fields and set a time to follow up. Another is to agree on the definitions before sending a complete quote. Either person can propose either option.

Consider both what the client can use now and how the final figures will be checked. A partial quote can be useful if its limits are clear. Waiting can avoid comparing figures with different meanings, but it may leave the client without the information they need for a meeting.

Record which definitions are agreed, which figures were cleared for release and who will resolve each question. This tests the quality of the handover. It cannot identify someone as ESFJ or ISTJ.

### ### ESFJ and ISTJ: a relative asks about trade pricing

In a fictional supply business, a relative who runs a small grocery shop asks about trade pricing and an invoice. Two colleagues have the same information and the same authority to refer the request for review. Neither can approve a discount.

One concern is how granting or refusing an exception would affect the relative, other customers and colleagues. Another is how the same criteria would apply to comparable requests. Either employee can consider both before explaining what is possible.

Either person can decline a request they cannot approve and, where appropriate, explain the usual route for checking eligibility. The way they phrase that answer does not reveal how much they care.

The two colleagues could reach the same decision for different reasons, or include both reasons. The example shows what each consideration would add, without assigning that consideration to a type.
sections.title: ESFJ and ISTJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
A person can care how a decision affects a client and still want the same criteria applied across cases. An ISTJ’s Thinking preference does not describe their warmth, and an ESFJ’s Feeling preference does not say whether they will make an exception.

Both people can hold to a definition or refer a special case for approval. Knowing who has authority and what the rules allow matters more than inferring a preference from the outcome.

A careful table may reflect training, a template or the demands of an audit. It does not establish a preference.

Calling first or checking records first can depend on what information is missing, how much time remains and who is responsible for the reply. Either type can do both.
sections.title: ESFJ and ISTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
If two results differ, compare the instruments, versions, languages and scoring. Consider whether you answered with similar experiences in mind. The labels alone cannot establish what changed.

For reflection, choose several situations where you had a genuine choice. Note how you worked through the issue, which criteria mattered and what the role required. Include a situation where you took a different approach.

Use the notes to describe your own experience. They cannot assign a type, quantify your resemblance to a profile or validate a test result.
sections.title: ESFJ and ISTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
For E/I, a person could clarify the same issue in conversation or by reflecting privately. For T/F, they could weigh the effect on the client or how consistently the definitions apply.

Either person might use all those considerations. Which question they ask first can depend on the task and the information available.
items.question: ### How might ESFJ and ISTJ approach the same quote?

items.answer:
Si is auxiliary for ESFJ and dominant for ISTJ. The notation here uses Ne as ESFJ’s tertiary Intuition. It is ISTJ’s inferior function. The match on Ne depends on the tertiary notation.

The judging functions also differ under this convention: ESFJ uses dominant Fe and inferior Ti, while ISTJ uses auxiliary Te and tertiary Fi. Sharing a function does not establish which records two people will consult or what they will conclude.
items.question: ### Why do ESFJ and ISTJ share Si and Ne in the displayed stacks?

items.answer:
Yes. Either person can explain a rule clearly and take account of how it affects the client.

A person’s responsibilities, experience and authority can shape the response. Neither the wording nor the decision to make an exception can establish a type.
items.question: ### Can an ISTJ consider a client’s feelings and an ESFJ keep to a rule?

items.answer:
Yes. The work depends on checking figures, clarifying definitions and communicating decisions. Assign it according to access, authority and skill.

To explore the work, try mapping a fictional quote to a client’s template and explaining which lines still need confirmation. Compare your experience with the tasks in an actual procurement or account role.
items.question: ### Can either type prepare quotes and reconcile figures?

items.answer:
Clarify which parts the client can use now and which still need approval. Agree on a time to follow up.

If a partial submission is appropriate, send only verified figures cleared for release. Mark the missing fields and explain when you expect to complete them. This can work for either type.
items.question: ### How can ESFJ and ISTJ agree on when to send a quote?

items.answer:
They differ on E/I and T/F. Compare how the instruments ask about those preferences and whether you had similar situations in mind when you answered.

If the instrument explains its scores and cutoffs, use its guidance to interpret the result. The labels alone cannot tell you how close either score was to a threshold. Keep the distinction between what a role required and what you would choose in similar circumstances.
